tools.name: get_ticket
tools.description: Get one ticket in full, including its description and its project and swimlane context, plus its comments. Use this before update_ticket so you are editing from the current text rather than overwriting it. The ticket's `key` (e.g. CM-00001) is what people call it by — quote that rather than the UUID when reporting back. For an initiative this is also the only place its contents are listed: the project tools hide them.

key.description: The ticket's key, e.g. CM-00001. Case and zero-padding don't matter, so CM-1 works too. Use this when a person gave you a key rather than a UUID.

tools.name: set_ticket_risk
tools.description: Rate how risky a ticket is against one named criterion from a rubric declared in code. A rating is two things and needs both: a level, which says how worried to be, and a rationale, which says why — the level on its own is an assertion nobody can check. Advisory, and it refuses nothing. No ticket is blocked, gated, reordered or re-typed because of a rating, and rating a ticket high does not stop anybody implementing it: this records a judgement for a person to read, and that is all it does. One call rates one criterion, and the rubric has five, so a full assessment is five calls — there is deliberately no argument for sending them together. Rating a criterion again replaces what was there, with the previous level and rationale kept in full in the ticket's audit trail; nothing clears a rating, so correct yourself by calling again rather than looking for a way to send null. Read before you write: get_ticket returns the ticket's current ratings under `risk`, so look at what somebody has already recorded instead of assuming the rubric is empty.

criterion.description: Which question you are answering. blast_radius — how far the damage from a mistake would spread — one template's copy is narrow, a service every request passes through is wide; reversibility — how hard the change would be to undo once shipped; a change that cannot be rolled back rates high; data_and_migration — what the change does to data that already exists — a nullable column with nothing to backfill is low, a backfill that guesses or anything that drops a column is high; security_and_authorization — whether the change touches who may see or do what — organization scoping, project roles, sessions, MCP scopes, or any path that renders text somebody else wrote; external_dependency — how much the change leans on something outside Abacus that can fail or change without warning — GitHub, SMTP, an OAuth client, a skill in another repo on its own release cycle.

level.description: How risky this ticket is on that question. low — a mistake on this criterion would be small, obvious, or easily undone; medium — real exposure that ordinary care covers; name it so a reviewer can see it was considered; high — this is where the change could hurt; say what would go wrong and what has to hold for it not to.

rationale.description: Why that level, in markdown source. Required — a level with no argument behind it cannot be weighed by anybody reading it later. This is the argument for the level, not the design document the argument came out of, so keep it to the reasoning.

tools.name: record_metric
tools.description: Record that something measurable happened to a ticket — most often, that you ran a skill against it. Abacus cannot observe this: nothing outside your own run knows a skill started, so if you do not record it, it did not happen as far as the ticket is concerned. Record it ONCE, when you finish, not on every turn and not when you begin — a skill that reports each time it thinks makes the count meaningless. If you were interrupted and never finished, record nothing. Measurements accumulate and are never edited or deleted, by you or by anybody: get this right rather than expecting to correct it. Read the summary back with get_ticket.

ticket_id.description: The ticket the work was done on.

metric.description: What kind of measurement this is. skill_invoked — somebody ran an agent skill against this ticket. The subject is the bare skill name, without the plugin or the leading slash.

subject.description: What the measurement is of, in lowercase words joined by single hyphens — for skill_invoked, the bare skill name (gather-requirements), never the whole command. Required for a metric that names a subject above, and refused for one that does not.

value.description: How much, in the unit the metric names. Defaults to 1, which is what a single run is — pass this only to report several at once, or an amount.

note.description: Optional one-line context, shown beside the entry in the ticket's activity feed. Anything longer belongs in a comment.

tools.name: list_projects
tools.description: List every project in the organization with its swimlane and ticket counts. Start here when you don't yet know which project to work on; the returned project ids are what every other tool takes. Each project also carries the ticket_prefix its keys use, e.g. CM.

tools.name: list_tickets
tools.description: List a project's tickets as a flat array, newest position first within each swimlane, optionally narrowed to one swimlane or one assignee. Prefer this over get_project when you want to filter or count rather than understand the project's layout. Tickets inside an initiative are not listed unless you ask for that initiative by id.

project_id.description: The project whose tickets to list.

swimlane_id.description: Only return tickets in this swimlane.

assignee_id.description: Only return tickets assigned to this member.

unassigned_only.description: Only return tickets with no assignee.

initiative_id.description: Only return the tickets filed under this initiative. Without it you get the project's own tickets and no initiative's contents — an initiative is listed as one ticket, carrying the counts that say how much is inside it.

tools.name: add_comment
tools.description: Write a comment on a ticket. Use this to record what you did, what you found, or a question for the assignee — anything that belongs in the discussion rather than in the ticket's own description. Comments you write are visibly attributed to the agent, alongside the person whose access you are using, so say things you would be happy to have quoted back. Editing and deleting comments is not available to agents; only the person who wrote a comment can do that, in the web UI.

body.description: What to say. Plain text; line breaks are kept.
